context: You work in a company and you received a letter from the HR manager.

paragraphs: I want to inform you that we have decided to allow some workers to work from their homes.
What do you think about this plan? Can this plan bring any benefits for workers and for the company? We appreciate your opinion very much.

part2_question: Why is the crime rate increasing among teenagers?

task11: Big news at work: HR is going to let some people work from home. I am really pleased, because the daily commute takes two hours of my life. I hope they include my department, as I concentrate far better at my own desk. How does it work at your office?
task12: Thank you for your letter about the new policy on working from home. I welcome the decision and believe it can benefit both staff and the company.

For employees, the clearest gain is time. Without a long commute, people arrive at work rested, and many of us concentrate better at home, where there are fewer interruptions than in an open-plan office. For the company, that usually means higher productivity, better morale and lower office costs.

I would therefore like to ask that my own role be considered for the scheme. Most of my work is done on a computer, and with a reliable internet connection and a weekly team meeting I am confident I could do it just as effectively from home.
part2: The rise in crime among teenagers is a serious problem, and I do not think a single cause can explain it.

One factor is the influence of the internet. Young people are exposed to violent material long before they are mature enough to judge it, and constant exposure can make aggression look ordinary rather than shocking.

A second and probably stronger factor is social and economic. Poverty, unstable homes and the absence of adult supervision create exactly the conditions in which crime grows. A teenager from a disadvantaged background who sees no realistic future may turn to theft out of desperation rather than choice. Where a family is struggling simply to pay for food and rent, children are often left to supervise themselves for most of the day.

A third factor is untreated mental illness. Depression and anxiety that nobody notices can express themselves as anti-social or destructive behaviour. Boys in particular are far less likely than girls to ask for help when something is wrong.
In short, the problem has several roots and will not be solved by punishment alone. Support for struggling families, better schooling and real opportunities are all part of the answer.
